articles.title: Scientists discover that a clogged filter could revolutionize oil refining
articles.summary: Scientists have developed a remarkable new membrane that separates crude oil at room temperature, using the oil itself to create microscopic filtration channels. The breakthrough could cut refining energy consumption by nearly 32%, carbon emissions by almost 38%, and operating costs by 36%, potentially transforming one of the world's most energy-intensive industries.
articles.content:
Researchers have developed a surprisingly simple way to separate crude oil without heating it, potentially transforming one of the world's most energy-intensive industrial processes. The breakthrough uses an inexpensive membrane that could significantly reduce the energy required for oil refining while lowering operating costs and carbon emissions.

The international research effort was led by Professor Dong-Yeun Koh at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, known as KAIST, in collaboration with Professor Ryan Lively's research group at Georgia Tech. KAIST(President Kwang Hyung Lee) announced that the team had successfully demonstrated a membrane capable of separating crude oil at room temperature. The findings were published in Nature, one of the world's leading scientific journals.

Crude oil is essential for far more than gasoline and other transportation fuels. It also supplies the raw materials used to manufacture plastics, packaging, clothing, and numerous everyday products. Because refining costs affect the prices of these materials, making the process more efficient could have widespread economic and environmental benefits.

Why Traditional Crude Oil Refining Requires So Much Energy

For more than a century, oil refineries have relied heavily on distillation to separate crude oil into useful components. The process involves heating oil to temperatures above 350 °C, turning portions of it into vapor, and then cooling those vapors to collect different fractions.

This approach requires an enormous amount of energy. Worldwide, crude oil distillation consumes approximately 1,100 terawatt-hours (TWh) annually. That is comparable to the combined yearly electricity production of roughly 130 continuously operating nuclear power plants, each with a capacity of about one gigawatt.

The massive energy demand makes distillation a major contributor to both fuel consumption and greenhouse gas emissions within the refining industry. Meanwhile, growing economic pressures across global petrochemical markets have increased interest in technologies that can separate oil more efficiently.

Membranes have emerged as a promising alternative because they can separate substances without requiring the extreme temperatures used in conventional distillation. However, previous designs have faced significant obstacles.

Traditionally, researchers have assumed that effective molecular separation requires a membrane covered with an extremely thin, specialized coating. Although these coatings can provide the necessary precision, they are expensive to produce and can develop defects when manufactured on a large scale. These limitations have made widespread industrial adoption difficult.

A Surprising Discovery Turns Clogged Filters Into an Advantage

The KAIST and Georgia Tech researchers approached the problem differently. Rather than adding a complicated coating, they used a bare membrane made from porous polyacrylonitrile (PAN), an inexpensive, chemically stable polymer already commonly used as a supporting material in industrial filtration systems.

What happened when crude oil passed through the membrane was unexpected.

As the oil flowed through its pores, heavier hydrocarbon molecules accumulated along the inner walls. This buildup gradually reduced the size of the openings, producing extremely narrow channels measuring less than 2 nanometers across.

In effect, the crude oil helped create the microscopic pathways needed to separate its own components.

These naturally formed channels allowed lighter oil fractions, including naphtha, gasoline, and kerosene, to pass through quickly while preventing heavier substances from traveling through the membrane as easily.

The discovery was especially surprising because the buildup of material inside membrane pores, known as fouling, is normally considered a serious problem. Fouling typically reduces filtration performance and requires cleaning or replacement. In this case, however, the same phenomenon made the membrane highly effective at separating different molecules.

The results were impressive. The uncoated PAN membrane achieved crude oil permeation rates approximately 23 times higher than those reported for previous leading crude oil separation membranes. It also continued operating with stable performance for 28 consecutive days.

Professor Ryan Lively (Georgia Tech) commented: "One of the key challenges facing membrane systems for crude oil separation was the low productivities of the membrane units -- the PAN membranes with their surprising separation mechanism -- dramatically increase the productivity of the membrane unit, to the point where industry should seriously consider adopting the technology."

New Membrane Could Cut Oil Refining Energy Use by Nearly a Third

One of the technology's biggest advantages is that refineries would not necessarily need to replace their existing equipment to use it.

The membrane could instead be installed as a modular filtration system that processes crude oil before it enters conventional distillation equipment. This would reduce the amount of work required during the heating and separation stages while allowing facilities to continue using much of their current infrastructure.

Computer simulations suggest that incorporating the membrane into the refining process could deliver substantial improvements. Energy consumption could fall by 31.6%, while carbon dioxide emissions could decrease by 37.6%. The same calculations projected a 20.7% reduction in cooling water consumption and a 36% decrease in operating costs.

The potential environmental benefits could be considerable if the technology were adopted widely.

Researchers estimate that implementing the system throughout Korea's refining and petrochemical industries could prevent approximately 10 million tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions each year. That is roughly equivalent to the annual emissions produced by four million vehicles powered by internal combustion engines.

These savings are projections based on process simulations rather than reductions already demonstrated across operating refineries. Nevertheless, the findings suggest that membrane filtration could become a practical way to improve the efficiency of existing facilities.

Applications Beyond Oil Refining

Although crude oil separation was the main focus of the research, the same technology could eventually be useful in several other industries.

One potential application involves treating pyrolysis oil produced when waste plastics are broken down for recycling. The membranes could also help recover solvents used in battery manufacturing, purify pharmaceutical compounds, and improve biofuel production.

The broader opportunity lies in using complex liquid mixtures to help form the tiny filtration channels needed to separate their components. This approach could provide a more affordable and versatile alternative to conventional membranes that require precisely manufactured surface coatings.

Professor Dong-Yeun Koh of KAIST said, "This study reveals a new scientific principle in which a membrane interacts with a complex mixture and spontaneously forms its own separation channels. Working with real crude oil supplied by HD Hyundai Oilbank allowed us to validate the technology under conditions relevant to industrial operation."

The use of actual crude oil was an important part of the research because it allowed the team to examine how the membrane performed with the complicated mixture of hydrocarbons found in industrial feedstocks.

Before the technology can be deployed more widely, the researchers plan to improve membrane production at larger scales and establish its reliability during extended operation.

Professor Jae W. Lee of KAIST, a co-corresponding author of the study, added, "By advancing large-area membrane modularization and long-term operational reliability, we hope to broaden the adoption of membrane-based processes throughout the refining and petrochemical industries."

Dr. Jihoon Choi and Dr. Hyeokjun Seo of KAIST, the study's co-first authors, said, "Our goal is to precisely control this spontaneous pore-constriction phenomenon and develop it into a membrane platform applicable to the entire refining process. We also aim to expand the technology to plastic recycling, biofuel purification, and other sustainable chemical processes that support carbon neutrality."

The research received support from Korea's Ministry of Science and ICT through the Basic Research Program for Outstanding Early-Career Researchers and the Engineering Research Center (ERC) Program.

articles.personality_title: New membrane technology could cut oil refining energy use by nearly a third
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Crude oil is used to make fuels and many everyday products, but refining it requires heating the oil to very high temperatures. This heating uses a huge amount of energy and creates lots of carbon emissions, making oil refining one of the most energy-heavy industries.

**What happened** – Scientists from Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) and Georgia Tech developed a new, simple membrane filter that can separate crude oil at room temperature. Instead of heating, this membrane uses the oil itself to form tiny channels that separate lighter parts like gasoline from heavier parts. The discovery was surprising because normally clogged filters are a problem, but here the clogging helps the filter work better.

**Impact** – This new membrane could reduce the energy used in refining by about 32%, cut carbon emissions by nearly 38%, and lower operating costs by 36%. If widely used, it could prevent millions of tons of greenhouse gases yearly, helping reduce environmental damage from oil refining.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A new membrane filter that uses crude oil to create its own tiny separation channels could make oil refining cheaper, cleaner, and more energy-efficient without needing major changes to existing factories.

articles.personality_presentation_fr:

**Impact** – Cette nouvelle membrane pourrait réduire d’environ 32 % l’énergie utilisée pour le raffinage, diminuer les émissions de carbone de près de 38 % et baisser les coûts d’exploitation de 36 %. **Résumé en une phrase** – Un nouveau filtre membrane qui utilise le pétrole brut pour créer ses propres canaux microscopiques pourrait rendre le raffinage du pétrole moins cher, plus propre et plus économe en énergie sans nécessiter de modifications majeures des usines actuelles.

articles.title: Hydrogen Derivatives Enable Cost-Effective Carbon Neutrality in China
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 05 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11351-4Hydrogen Derivatives Enable Cost-Effective Carbon Neutrality in China
articles.content: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change recommended 1.5°C carbon reduction target, requiring powerful enforcement from major economies. China, the largest CO 2 emitter, is facing severe difficulties for both variable renewable accommodation and decarbonization of hard-to-abate sectors. Hydrogen, as a critical green energy carrier bridging renewable to end-users, faces significant obstacles in real-world deployment such as costly transportation, storage and fuel-cell adoption. Affordable and coordinated hydrogen deployment plan to accelerate the carbon-neutral transition remains ambiguous. Here, we present cost-effective carbon-neutral transition pathways for entire energy economy of China emphasizing the significant role of hydrogen and derivatives as green energy carriers, considering high-resolution renewable deployments, hourly power system operations in 29 provincial regions, over 46,000 rail/road/marine/pipeline transfer routing of hydrogen derivatives, process-level fuel adoption strategies in all end-use sectors. Results show that incorporating hydrogen and derivatives can reduce the overall transition cost by $ 10.7 trillion compared with renewable and electrification pathways, achieving negative carbon abatement costs ($-6.15/ton), eliminating external oil import expenses, equivalent to over 50% of China trade surplus (2023 level)1, significantly boosting employment and economic growth. Hydrogen derivative based transition pathway offers a vital direction for affordable and secure decarbonization for China and beyond under volatile international energy markets.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific and economic breakthrough showing that hydrogen derivatives can enable a cost-effective carbon-neutral transition for China's entire energy economy. This has broad positive implications for climate action, economic growth, and energy security in the world's largest CO2 emitter, with detailed analysis and measurable benefits.
articles.personality_title: Hydrogen helps China cut carbon costs and boost economy
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – China is the world's largest emitter of carbon dioxide, and it faces big challenges in reducing emissions and using renewable energy effectively. Hydrogen, a clean energy carrier, could help but is expensive and hard to use on a large scale.

**What happened** – Scientists studied how using hydrogen and its derivatives (related energy forms) could help China reach carbon neutrality. They analyzed detailed data from 29 regions, including how to produce, transport, and use hydrogen in different sectors. Their results show that using hydrogen can lower the overall cost of switching to clean energy by $10.7 trillion compared to other methods.

**Impact** – This approach not only cuts carbon emissions but also saves money, creates jobs, and boosts economic growth. It reduces China’s need to import oil, saving money equal to half of China’s trade surplus in 2023. This shows hydrogen can be a practical and affordable way to fight climate change while helping the economy.

**What's next step** – The study’s findings suggest China and other countries can focus on building hydrogen infrastructure and policies to support this cleaner energy path. Future work will likely involve turning these plans into real projects and expanding hydrogen use across industries.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Using hydrogen energy can make China’s path to carbon neutrality cheaper, cleaner, and better for the economy.

articles.title: Solar kits are changing what disaster relief looks like
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Every morning in the camp at Teknaf, Bangladesh, Mohammed Saber climbs to the roof of his family’s bamboo-and-tarpaulin home and sets out a single rectangular solar panel. He has done this for six years, since his family fled the Myanmar military’s crackdown on the Rohingya people in 2017. “We […]
The post Solar kits are changing what disaster relief looks like first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

Every morning in the camp at Teknaf, Bangladesh, Mohammed Saber climbs to the roof of his family’s bamboo-and-tarpaulin home and sets out a single rectangular solar panel. He has done this for six years, since his family fled the Myanmar military’s crackdown on the Rohingya people in 2017. “We can now charge our phones, cook with light, children can study at night and use fans during the hot season,” says Saber, 35. A small panel on a makeshift roof, and an entire household runs on it.

The same thing is happening in camps and disaster zones around the world. Solar has been edging into humanitarian response for years; what’s shifted is how seriously organizations are taking it, less as an experiment and more as something people actually need.

From lanterns to cook stoves

The range of what “solar kit” means is wider than it might sound. Sarah Rosenberg-Jansen, a research fellow at the Stockholm Environment Institute, describes the category as spanning solar lanterns, torches, and heating pads to full solar home systems and electric cook stoves. The common thread is portability and independence from the grid, which matters most when infrastructure is gone and things are moving fast. “In emergency situations, solar kits can be deployed immediately,” she says.

That’s playing out across multiple places at once. In Karachi, Doctors Without Borders runs a tuberculosis clinic on solar power. In South Sudan’s Renk County, the UN migration agency installed solar-powered water filtration for families displaced by the war in neighboring Sudan. When Nepal’s floods killed 1,455 people and left 5,285 missing in August, local and international organizations distributed solar kits to survivors cut off from the grid. In Ukraine, a nonprofit called Hope For Ukraine has provided kits to thousands of families living through a war, including older residents who adapted without trouble. “We have grandmas and grandpas who are around 75 to 80 years old receiving kits,” says CEO Yuriy Boyechko. “It’s just a matter of plug and play.”

Why costs finally shifted

Solar panels don’t carry the same price volatility as fossil fuels, which are expensive and difficult to transport into disaster zones under ordinary circumstances and near-impossible when infrastructure has been destroyed. Only a few decades ago, solar was a luxury technology. Mass manufacturing and steady advances in efficiency changed that, and the price drop put solar kits within reach of humanitarian budgets in ways they weren’t before.

Funding cuts and the waiting list

What’s slowing things down now isn’t the technology. Aid organizations have long-running contracts built around diesel generators, and switching to solar means trusting new equipment, building new distribution chains, and sometimes doing that in genuinely hazardous conditions. Mark Gibson of the Global Platform for Action, a group promoting clean energy access, notes that the transition has been complicated for organizations with established logistics in place.

Cuts to international donor funding have made it harder. Aimee Jenks, a program leader at GPA, was direct: “Much of the technical expertise in the humanitarian sector on energy has been cut. That’s now retracting a lot of progress.”

Hope For Ukraine’s own numbers show how stretched the system is. By the end of 2026, the organization expects to have distributed more than 3,200 solar kits, a number that took two years to reach because of funding. “We have a waiting list of about 20,000 families,” Boyechko says. “We just cannot keep up with demand.”

For Saber, the gap between what’s available and what people have isn’t an abstraction. His family has had their panel for six years, long enough to know exactly what changed. “It’s improved my family’s life,” he says.

Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary.

Los recortes en financiamiento han frenado la entrega de kits solares. Grupos como Hope For Ukraine tienen listas de espera con miles de familias que aún esperan su kit. Más apoyo y fondos podrían acelerar este cambio.

**Resumen en una frase** – Los kits solares portátiles están proporcionando energía limpia y confiable a familias en zonas de desastre, mejorando su vida diaria y mostrando una nueva forma más rápida y ecológica de brindar ayuda.

articles.title: 'Extra special' tamarin twins born at zoo
articles.summary: Shaldon Wildlife Trust says it is one of two European zoos to breed the species in 2026.
articles.content:
One of the UK's smallest accredited zoos is celebrating after "extra special" pied tamarin twins were born at the site.

Shaldon Wildlife Trust, in Devon, said the critically endangered twins were born on 29 September to mum Bobby and dad Pedra. Its director, Zak Showell, said it was a "challenge" to breed the species.

The trust said the animals were among the most endangered primates in South America. Bosses said the infants were "thriving" and had started to hitch rides on their parents' backs as they explored their habitat.

Showell said: "For a zoo of our size to achieve this and to be one of just two European zoos to manage it this year is an unbelievable proud moment for our small team."
